Call the real readahead syscall on it. Does that alone bring the pages back in, or does a real read still have to happen first?

No read call happens at all — the syscall itself is enough.

lines.text: Run it for real: before readahead, not one of those pages was resident.
And immediately after that one call, every single one of them genuinely was.

lines.text: Those exact same, freshly cached pages: call a real hint to discard them.
Does that hint alone genuinely evict them, or is it merely advisory and simply ignored?
It genuinely evicts every single one of those pages.
A documented hint, once it's actually called, has a completely real effect.
Run it for real: every one of those pages was resident right after readahead.
And not a single one of them was resident right after that real discard call.

tolerated.line: Run it for real: every one of those pages was resident right after readahead.

lines.text: Read the same amount of data two genuinely different ways: once through a normal buffered read, once bypassing the cache entirely.
Does the bypassing read end up resident in the page cache too, or does it not?
Only the normal, buffered read ends up resident.
The bypassing read never touches that cache at all.

tolerated.line: Only the normal, buffered read ends up resident.

lines.text: Run it for real: the buffered read left every single page resident in the cache.
And the exact same read, bypassing the cache instead, left absolutely none resident.
If that discard hint can't evict a file's pages right after it's written,
what's actually stopping it?
Those pages are still dirty, and the hint only discards clean ones.
A page that hasn't been written back yet simply isn't eligible to be dropped.
The documentation is explicit: an unwritten, dirty page is never freed by that hint at all.
Flushing it to disk first is the only way to give the hint something clean to actually discard.

lines.text: So, pulling this together: bringing pages in early, pushing them back out, and never letting them in — these are really the same cache, pulled three different directions.
Who decides whether a given page is sitting in it right now.
So, pulling this topic together: one real syscall, called on its own, can refill a dropped file's residency before anyone reads a byte.
A second one empties those same pages back out, the instant they stop being dirty.
And a third path simply refuses.
It bypasses the cache completely.
